before.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

before.label: Quantitative history
before.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Historical demography; Robert Fogel and Douglass North in cliometrics. Further selections: Labrousse (1933), Benson (1961), Thernstrom (1964), Curtin (1969), Fogel and Engerman (1974), Gutman’s critique (1975).

strands.title: Occupations, property and social mobility
strands.focus: Separate occupational change from property accumulation through linked local records; Thernstrom’s use of Weber broadens class beyond a single occupational ranking.

strands.title: Slavery: estimates, coercion and interpretation
strands.focus: Read the cliometric study alongside Gutman’s criticism of its labor/cooperation interpretation; neither efficiency estimates nor a book’s polemical reception alone describe enslaved people’s lives.
strands.works: Time on the Cross (1974); Slavery and the Numbers Game (1975)

strands.title: Estimating the Atlantic slave trade
strands.focus: Reconstruct the scale of forced migration from uneven evidence. Curtin’s influential estimates were later revised; totals do not substitute for histories of violence and agency.
strands.works: The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969)

strands.title: Household surveys and the limits of response

outcomes.finding: Hajnal’s primary qualifications now accompany the marriage-pattern argument; Goody1983 explicitly questions uniqueness and comparative scale. Fleury/Henry1958 credits Goubert and other researchers while requiring a deliberate sample. Henry1978 distinguishes aggregate reconstruction from family subsets, and Biraben’s inventory coauthorship is independently located. The French method is not credited to an isolated founder.
outcomes.research_limit: Hajnal101–107 and selected conclusion130–135 OCR only; spreads interleave, tables not visually collated, middle and appendix not fully read. Goody8–9 only, his cited regional/ancient studies not independently audited. Fleury/Henry663–665 only;1956 manual metadata checked but body unread. Henry1978 five-page account read, underlying records and estimates not replicated. Biraben1960 coauthorship metadata only. No complete regional survey, universal fertility mechanism or demonstrated marriage-to-growth causation.
